query: Which material can be used for improve the magnetocaloric properties, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating interstitial dopants (e.g., oxygen or nitrogen) into a Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–Ti high‐entropy alloy will induce lattice distortions that enhance magnetic interactions and increase the magnetocaloric effect.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic refractory high‐entropy alloy (e.g., Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi) in a random solid solution state.
generation.intervention: Introduce controlled amounts of interstitial oxygen (or nitrogen) during synthesis to dope the HEA.
generation.conditions: Measurements performed under cyclic magnetic field application over the temperature range where magnetic transitions are expected.
generation.structural_mediator: The interstitial atoms create local lattice distortions and modify the electronic environment.
generation.mechanism: The local distortions and altered bonding environments modulate the magnetic exchange interactions and may increase the magnetic entropy change when an external magnetic field is applied, thereby enhancing the magnetocaloric effect.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the undoped base alloy, the interstitial-doped HEA is predicted to exhibit an increased magnetic entropy change and improved cooling capacity under applied magnetic fields.
generation.baseline: The magnetocaloric properties of the undoped, equiatomic Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi HEA.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected to be specific to HEAs with similar compositions and synthesis conditions; the magnitude of enhancement remains uncertain and may depend on the exact dopant concentration and processing parameters.
generation.uncertainty: The precise size of the magnetocaloric improvement is uncertain, as the direct link between interstitial-induced lattice distortions and magnetocaloric performance in these complex alloys is not yet well established.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of samples: one set of the base Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi HEA and another set doped with a controlled amount of oxygen (or nitrogen). Characterize both sets structurally (using XRD and TEM to assess lattice distortions) and magnetically (via magnetization vs temperature measurements and magnetic entropy change (ΔSm) analysis under cyclic magnetic fields).
measurements: X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to measure lattice distortions
Magnetic entropy change (ΔSm) measurements using magnetization data under varying magnetic field strengths
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the interstitial-doped samples do not show a statistically significant increase in magnetic entropy change (or other magnetocaloric parameters) relative to the undoped samples, then the hypothesis that interstitial doping enhances magnetocaloric properties in this HEA is falsified.

Unlike other conventional alloys based on a “principal element,” high-entropy alloy (HEA) is a unique material that maintains a random solid solution structure without forming intermetallic compounds in operating temperatures due to its high configurational entropy [1] – [3] . It also has outstanding physical and chemical properties, which makes it a potential replacement for traditional metallic materials, and it has recently been referred to as a multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) or compositionally concentrated alloy (CCA) [4] – [9] .

As attention in HEAs increases, many studies have been conducted to explore its mechanical, physical and chemical properties [10] – [15] . In particular, equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, which was the first developed HEA, is the most studied because of its excellent combination of tensile strength and elongation along with excellent fracture toughness and corrosion resistance [6] , [16] – [21] . We observed that the relaxation peaks in the current HEAs are asymmetrically broadened (see Fig. 1, A to C ). This is a feature associated with the variety of interstitial relaxation processes involved in these massive solid solutions ( [28] ). Because of the complexity in alloy composition and the resulting multitude in local chemical environments in which the interstitial atoms switch their positions, it is difficult to conduct a complete peak deconvolution analysis based on all possible individual relaxation processes. However, two main configurations of the interstitial atoms can indeed be distinguished in the current material, namely, position switches of interstitials in ordered interstitial complexes and relaxation of randomly distributed interstitial atoms ( [22] ). These two kinds of configurations both contribute to the current Snoek relaxation and can cause at least some of the asymmetries observed. Therefore, we conduct a decomposition of the relaxation structure in terms of the two main classes of interstitial configurations (see the Supplementary Materials).
